# Editorial overview

All three problems use factorials and modular inverses under the prime modulus
`1,000,000,007`.

| Problem | Formula |
|---|---|
| A. Choose Queries | `C(n,k)` |
| B. Rearrange Letters | `n! / product(count!)` |
| C. Distribute Candies | `C(n+s-1,n-1)` |

# Factorial helper

Precompute:

```text
fact[i] = i!
invfact[i] = inverse(i!)
```

Then:

```text
C(n,k) = fact[n] * invfact[k] * invfact[n-k] mod MOD
```

# A. Choose Queries

## Restatement

Answer many binomial coefficient queries modulo `MOD`.

## Algorithm

Read all queries, find the largest `n`, precompute factorials and inverse
factorials up to that limit, then answer each query in `O(1)`.

## Correctness proof

`fact[n]` stores `n!`. Since `MOD` is prime and `n < MOD`, the factorials in the
denominator are invertible. Multiplying by `invfact[k]` and `invfact[n-k]` is
therefore exactly division by `k!(n-k)!` in modular arithmetic. This matches
the binomial coefficient formula. `\square`

## Complexity

```text
Preprocessing: O(max n)
Each query:   O(1)
Memory:       O(max n)
```

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

const long long MOD = 1000000007LL;

long long mod_pow(long long a, long long b) {
    long long result = 1;
    while (b > 0) {
        if (b & 1LL) result = result * a % MOD;
        a = a * a % MOD;
        b >>= 1LL;
    }
    return result;
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int q;
    if (!(cin >> q)) return 0;
    vector<pair<int, int>> queries(q);
    int limit = 0;
    for (auto &[n, k] : queries) {
        cin >> n >> k;
        limit = max(limit, n);
    }
    vector<long long> fact(limit + 1, 1), invfact(limit + 1, 1);
    for (int i = 1; i <= limit; i++) fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % MOD;
    invfact[limit] = mod_pow(fact[limit], MOD - 2);
    for (int i = limit; i >= 1; i--) invfact[i - 1] = invfact[i] * i % MOD;
    for (auto [n, k] : queries) {
        cout << fact[n] * invfact[k] % MOD * invfact[n - k] % MOD << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


MOD = 1_000_000_007


def prepare(limit: int) -> tuple[list[int], list[int]]:
    fact = [1] * (limit + 1)
    for i in range(1, limit + 1):
        fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % MOD
    invfact = [1] * (limit + 1)
    invfact[limit] = pow(fact[limit], MOD - 2, MOD)
    for i in range(limit, 0, -1):
        invfact[i - 1] = invfact[i] * i % MOD
    return fact, invfact
```

# B. Rearrange Letters

## Restatement

Count distinct permutations of all letters in a string that may contain
repeated letters.

## Observations

There are `n!` permutations if every position were distinguishable. For a
letter that appears `c` times, permutations among those equal copies are not
distinct, so divide by `c!`.

## Formula

```text
answer = n! / product(count[ch]!)
```

## Correctness proof

Label equal letters temporarily. There are `n!` labeled permutations. For any
fixed final string, the `count[ch]` copies of each character can be permuted
among themselves without changing the visible string, giving exactly
`product(count[ch]!)` labeled permutations for the same visible arrangement.
Dividing gives the number of distinct arrangements. Modular inverses implement
the same division under `MOD`. `\square`

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

const long long MOD = 1000000007LL;

long long mod_pow(long long a, long long b) {
    long long result = 1;
    while (b > 0) {
        if (b & 1LL) result = result * a % MOD;
        a = a * a % MOD;
        b >>= 1LL;
    }
    return result;
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    string s;
    if (!(cin >> s)) return 0;
    int n = (int)s.size();
    vector<long long> fact(n + 1, 1);
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % MOD;
    vector<int> cnt(26, 0);
    for (char ch : s) cnt[ch - 'a']++;
    long long answer = fact[n];
    for (int c : cnt) answer = answer * mod_pow(fact[c], MOD - 2) % MOD;
    cout << answer << '\n';
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


MOD = 1_000_000_007


def main() -> None:
    data = sys.stdin.buffer.read().strip()
    if not data:
        return
    n = len(data)
    fact = [1] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % MOD
    counts = [0] * 26
    for ch in data:
        counts[ch - 97] += 1
    answer = fact[n]
    for c in counts:
        answer = answer * pow(fact[c], MOD - 2, MOD) % MOD
    print(answer)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

# C. Distribute Candies

## Restatement

Count nonnegative integer solutions:

```text
x1 + x2 + ... + xn = s
```

## Stars-and-bars derivation

Represent candies by stars and separators between children by bars. There are
`s` stars and `n-1` bars, so `s+n-1` positions. Choosing the bar positions
uniquely determines the distribution.

Therefore:

```text
answer = C(s+n-1, n-1)
```

## Correctness proof

Given a distribution, write `x1` stars, then a bar, then `x2` stars, and so on.
This creates a unique sequence of `s` stars and `n-1` bars. Conversely, any such
sequence determines how many stars lie in each of the `n` gaps. This is a
bijection, so the number of distributions is the number of ways to choose the
bar positions: `C(s+n-1,n-1)`. `\square`

## Full C++ solution

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

const long long MOD = 1000000007LL;

long long mod_pow(long long a, long long b) {
    long long result = 1;
    while (b > 0) {
        if (b & 1LL) result = result * a % MOD;
        a = a * a % MOD;
        b >>= 1LL;
    }
    return result;
}

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false);
    cin.tie(nullptr);

    int q;
    if (!(cin >> q)) return 0;
    vector<pair<int, int>> queries(q);
    int limit = 0;
    for (auto &[n, s] : queries) {
        cin >> n >> s;
        limit = max(limit, n + s - 1);
    }
    vector<long long> fact(limit + 1, 1), invfact(limit + 1, 1);
    for (int i = 1; i <= limit; i++) fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % MOD;
    invfact[limit] = mod_pow(fact[limit], MOD - 2);
    for (int i = limit; i >= 1; i--) invfact[i - 1] = invfact[i] * i % MOD;
    for (auto [n, s] : queries) {
        int total = n + s - 1;
        int choose = n - 1;
        cout << fact[total] * invfact[choose] % MOD * invfact[total - choose] % MOD << '\n';
    }
    return 0;
}
```

## Full Python solution

```python
import sys


MOD = 1_000_000_007


def prepare(limit: int) -> tuple[list[int], list[int]]:
    fact = [1] * (limit + 1)
    for i in range(1, limit + 1):
        fact[i] = fact[i - 1] * i % MOD
    invfact = [1] * (limit + 1)
    invfact[limit] = pow(fact[limit], MOD - 2, MOD)
    for i in range(limit, 0, -1):
        invfact[i - 1] = invfact[i] * i % MOD
    return fact, invfact
```

# Testing discussion

The random tests compare against Python's exact `math.comb` and exact
factorial arithmetic for small cases, then reduce modulo `MOD`. Important cases
include:

```text
k = 0 and k = n
s = 0
n = 1
all letters equal
all letters distinct
```

# What to carry forward

Most beginner combinatorics under modulo reduces to:

```text
precompute factorials
precompute inverse factorials
translate the story into C(n,k), duplicate permutations, or stars-and-bars
```

The next section adds inclusion-exclusion for cases where direct counting
overcounts invalid objects.
